claim: Precursor tRNAs (pre-tRNAs) are transcribed by RNA Polymerase III with a 5′ leader and a 3′ trailer sequence.
source: Precursor tRNAs (pre-tRNAs) are first transcribed by RNA Polymerase III with a 5′ leader and a 3′ trailer sequence (Guerrier-Takada et al., 1983; Cook et al., 2009; Skowronek et al., 2014; Harris, 2016; Graczyk et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Pre-tRNAs must be end matured and modified, spliced, amino-acylated, and exported from the nucleus in eukaryotes to function in translation.
source: To function in translation, pre-tRNAs must be end matured and modified, spliced, amino-acylated, and exported from the nucleus in eukaryotes.
evidence: Draws from established understanding of tRNA processing requirements

claim: Steps in tRNA processing are not necessarily sequential.
source: Importantly, it has come to be appreciated that these steps in tRNA processing are not necessarily sequential (Trotta et al., 1997; Yoshihisa et al., 2003; Yoshihisa et al., 2007; Wu and Hopper, 2014; Hopper and Huang, 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Phizicky and Hopper, 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, intron-containing tRNAs are spliced in the cytoplasm on the mitochondrial surface by the tRNA Splicing Endonuclease (SEN) complex following nuclear export.
source: For example, in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, intron-containing tRNAs are spliced in the cytoplasm on the mitochondrial surface by the tRNA Splicing Endonuclease (SEN) complex following nuclear export (Yoshihisa et al., 2003; Yoshihisa et al., 2007; Skowronek et al., 2014; Wan and Hopper, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Cytoplasmic tRNAs can be reimported to the nucleus through retrograde transport to allow tRNAs to undergo further modification and quality control.
source: Furthermore, cytoplasmic tRNAs can be reimported to the nucleus through retrograde transport to allow tRNAs to undergo further modification and quality control which is also used to repress translation during conditions of stress (Murthi et al., 2010; Hopper and Huang, 2015; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Retrograde transport of tRNAs is used to repress translation during conditions of stress.
source: Furthermore, cytoplasmic tRNAs can be reimported to the nucleus through retrograde transport to allow tRNAs to undergo further modification and quality control which is also used to repress translation during conditions of stress (Murthi et al., 2010; Hopper and Huang, 2015; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: tRNAs undergo various chemical modifications that are spatially regulated as they cycle between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: As tRNAs cycle between the nucleus and cytoplasm, they undergo various chemical modifications that are also spatially regulated (Phizicky and Hopper, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: End maturation and amino-acylation are required for recognition by the tRNA Exportin Los1/Exportin-t and Msn5, respectively.
source: In the context of nuclear export, end maturation and amino-acylation are required for recognition by the tRNA Exportin Los1/Exportin-t and Msn5, respectively (Huang and Hopper, 2015; Chatterjee et al., 2017; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020; Chatterjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Los1 and Msn5 are non-essential and can be deleted in combination.
source: Although Los1 and Msn5 are the best characterized tRNA export factors, both are non-essential and can be deleted in combination (Takano et al., 2005; Murthi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The karyopherin Crm1 and mobile nucleoporin Mex67 have functional roles in regulating tRNA nucleocytoplasmic dynamics.
source: These studies have elucidated functional roles of the karyopherin Crm1 and mobile nucleoporin Mex67 in regulating tRNA nucleocytoplasmic dynamics (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Derrer et al., 2019; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020; Chatterjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Crm1 and Mex67 have previously been shown to function in messenger RNA (mRNA) export.
source: Both factors have previously been shown to function in messenger RNA (mRNA) export (Hodge et al., 1999; Takemura et al., 2004; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Derrer et al., 2019), with Mex67 serving an essential role in the process (Hodge et al., 1999; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Adams and Wente, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Mex67 serves an essential role in mRNA export.
source: Both factors have previously been shown to function in messenger RNA (mRNA) export (Hodge et al., 1999; Takemura et al., 2004; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Derrer et al., 2019), with Mex67 serving an essential role in the process (Hodge et al., 1999; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Adams and Wente, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Crm1 and Mex67 both function parallel to Los1 to support export of pre-tRNA and re-export of spliced tRNA that have undergone retrograde transport.
source: In tRNA export, it is thought that Crm1 and Mex67 both function parallel to Los1 to support export of pre-tRNA and re-export of spliced tRNA that have undergone retrograde transport (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020; Chatterjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Mex67 serves a unique function in the premature export of pre-tRNAs that have not completed 5′ end processing.
source: Moreover, recent reports suggest subspecies specialization and family preferences for tRNA cargo, with Mex67 serving a unique function in the premature export of pre-tRNAs that have not completed 5′ end processing (Chatterjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mex67 and Crm1 have functions in pre-snRNA, pre-ribosomal subunit, and TLC1 (telomerase) export.
source: In addition to tRNA and mRNA, both Mex67 and Crm1 have functions in pre-snRNA, pre-ribosomal subunit, and TLC1 (telomerase) export (Yao et al., 2007; Faza et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014; Becker et al., 2019; Vasianovich et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 has been implicated in pre-snRNA, pre-ribosomal subunit, TLC1 (telomerase) export, and tRNA export.
source: Similarly, in addition to Mex67 and Crm1, the DEAD-box Protein 5 (Dbp5) has also been implicated in each of these RNA export pathways, including tRNA export (Wu et al., 2014; Neumann et al., 2016; Mikhailova et al., 2017; Becker et al., 2019; Lari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 is an RNA-stimulated ATPase that is spatially regulated by the nucleoporins Nup159 and Gle1 with the small molecule inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) at the cytoplasmic face of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) to promote the directional export of mRNA.
source: Dbp5 is most well known as an RNA-stimulated ATPase that is spatially regulated by the nucleoporins Nup159 and Gle1 with the small molecule inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) at the cytoplasmic face of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) to promote the directional export of mRNA (Snay-Hodge et al., 1998; Tseng et al., 1998; Hodge et al., 1999; Schmitt et al., 1999; Strahm et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2002; Weirich et al., 2004; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Alcázar-Román et al., 2006; Weirich et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2007; Dossani et al., 2009; Fan et al., 2009; von Moeller et al., 2009; Hodge et al., 2011, Montpetit et al., 2011; Noble et al., 2011; Kaminski et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2016; Adams et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2018; Adams and Wente, 2020).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm with reported roles in transcription, R-loop metabolism, and translation.
source: In addition to these export roles, Dbp5 also shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm with reported roles in transcription, R-loop metabolism, and translation (Hodge et al., 1999; Estruch and Cole, 2003; Gross et al., 2007; Scarcelli et al., 2008; Tieg and Krebber, 2013; Mikhailova et al., 2017; Lari et al., 2019; Beißel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Nup159 and Gle1 mutants alter tRNA export.
source: Notably, Nup159 and Gle1 mutants also alter tRNA export (Lari et al., 2019), suggesting the mRNA export pathway as a whole (e.g., Mex67, Dbp5, Gle1/InsP6, Nup159) may support tRNA export.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The dbp5L12A mutation disrupts a nuclear export sequence (NES) recognized by Crm1 to promote Dbp5 transport out of the nucleus.
source: Mutations were identified (e.g., dbp5L12A) that disrupt a nuclear export sequence (NES) recognized by Crm1 to promote Dbp5 transport out of the nucleus.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous mutagenesis screen

claim: The dbp5R423A mutant is impaired in nuclear import from the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast, another mutant, dbp5R423A, was found to be impaired in nuclear import from the cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous mutagenesis screen

claim: Neither dbp5L12A nor dbp5R423A mutations disrupt the essential mRNA export functions of Dbp5.
source: Importantly, neither of these mutations disrupt the essential mRNA export functions of Dbp5; however, limited nuclear access of dbp5R423A induced tRNA export defects, suggesting a potentially novel role for nuclear Dbp5 in tRNA export.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous mutagenesis screen

claim: Limited nuclear access of dbp5R423A induced tRNA export defects.
source: Importantly, neither of these mutations disrupt the essential mRNA export functions of Dbp5; however, limited nuclear access of dbp5R423A induced tRNA export defects, suggesting a potentially novel role for nuclear Dbp5 in tRNA export.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous mutagenesis screen

claim: A physical interaction between Dbp5 and tRNA was characterized, which was elevated upon nuclear accumulation of Dbp5 in a dbp5L12A mutant.
source: In support of this hypothesis, a physical interaction between Dbp5 and tRNA was also characterized, which was elevated upon nuclear accumulation of Dbp5 in a dbp5L12A mutant (Lari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In a los1Δ strain, the NPC localization of GFP-Dbp5 was not altered.
source: In a los1Δ, the NPC localization of GFP-Dbp5 was not altered (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: When Dbp5 loss of function was induced using auxin-induced degradation (AID), Los1-GFP localization remained unchanged.
source: Similarly, when a Dbp5 loss of function was induced using auxin-induced degradation (AID) (Nishimura et al., 2009), Los1-GFP localization remained unchanged (Figure 1B) while mRNA export defects were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), confirming depletion of Dbp5 to a level sufficient to disrupt mRNA export.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: mRNA export defects were detected upon Dbp5 depletion using auxin-induced degradation.
source: Similarly, when a Dbp5 loss of function was induced using auxin-induced degradation (AID) (Nishimura et al., 2009), Los1-GFP localization remained unchanged (Figure 1B) while mRNA export defects were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), confirming depletion of Dbp5 to a level sufficient to disrupt mRNA export.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Double mutants of los1Δ with dbp5L12A or dbp5R423A exhibited no growth defects.
source: Double mutants of los1Δ with dbp5L12A (increased in the nucleus) or dbp5R423 (depleted from the nucleus) exhibited no growth defects (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Combining dbp5L12A and dbp5R423A respectively with los1Δ/msn5Δ double mutants revealed minimal growth defects.
source: Similarly, combining dbp5L12A and dbp5R423A respectively with los1Δ/msn5Δ double mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) revealed minimal growth defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: The los1Δ dbp5R423A double mutant exhibited significantly stronger nuclear accumulation of pre-tRNA compared to single mutants or control after a 4 hr incubation at 37°C.
source: The los1Δ dbp5R423A double mutant exhibited significantly stronger nuclear accumulation of pre-tRNA compared to single mutants or control after a 4 hr incubation at 37°C (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: Elevating nuclear pools of Dbp5 by combining dbp5L12A with los1Δ did not alter the pre-tRNA export defects observed in los1Δ strains.
source: Notably, elevating nuclear pools of Dbp5 by combining dbp5L12A with los1Δ did not alter the pre-tRNA export defects observed in los1Δ strains, indicating that excess nuclear Dbp5 is not sufficient to suppress the los1Δ phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tRNA FISH experiments

claim: Excess nuclear Dbp5 is not sufficient to suppress the los1Δ phenotype.
source: Notably, elevating nuclear pools of Dbp5 by combining dbp5L12A with los1Δ did not alter the pre-tRNA export defects observed in los1Δ strains, indicating that excess nuclear Dbp5 is not sufficient to suppress the los1Δ phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no suppression of los1Δ phenotype

claim: Dbp5 has a role in pre-tRNA export that operates independently of Los1.
source: These data argue for a role for Dbp5 in pre-tRNA export that operates independently of Los1.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and FISH data showing additive defects in los1Δ dbp5R423A double mutants

claim: In a los1Δ strain, an approximately twofold reduction in the relative amount of pre-tRNA co-immunoprecipitated with Dbp5 was observed.
source: In a los1Δ strain, an approximately twofold reduction in the relative amount of pre-tRNA co-immunoprecipitated with Dbp5 (~9.5-fold enrichment in WT to ~4.5-fold in los1Δ) was observed, but importantly the deletion failed to abolish the Dbp5 pre-tRNA in vivo interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Loss of Los1 failed to abolish the Dbp5 pre-tRNA in vivo interaction.
source: In a los1Δ strain, an approximately twofold reduction in the relative amount of pre-tRNA co-immunoprecipitated with Dbp5 (~9.5-fold enrichment in WT to ~4.5-fold in los1Δ) was observed, but importantly the deletion failed to abolish the Dbp5 pre-tRNA in vivo interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Loss of Msn5 did not cause a significant change in Dbp5 pre-tRNA interactions by RNA IP.
source: Loss of Msn5, which does not have a published role in the export of intron-containing pre-tRNAs (Huang and Hopper, 2015), did not cause a significant change in Dbp5 pre-tRNA interactions by RNA IP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNA IP experiments

claim: Los1 may support Dbp5-pre-tRNA complex formation, but Dbp5 maintains an ability to bind pre-tRNA in vivo in the absence of Los1.
source: These results indicate that Los1 may support Dbp5-pre-tRNA complex formation, but Dbp5 maintains an ability to bind pre-tRNA in vivo in the absence of Los1.
evidence: Inferred from RNA IP data showing reduced but not abolished Dbp5-tRNA interaction in los1Δ

claim: Under conditions of Mex67-AA re-localization, no significant change in the Dbp5-tRNAIleUAU interaction was observed.
source: Under these conditions of Mex67-AA re-localization, no significant change in the Dbp5-tRNAIleUAU interaction was observed (median of ~8.8-fold enrichment before addition of rapamycin and ~8.2-fold after, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Nuclear retention of mRNAs via Mex67-AA resulted in strongly reduced binding of Dbp5 to the FBA1 mRNA.
source: Importantly, consistent with the function of Mex67 in mRNA export (Snay-Hodge et al., 1998; Tseng et al., 1998; Schmitt et al., 1999; Strahm et al., 1999; Weirich et al., 2004; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Tran et al., 2007; Dossani et al., 2009; von Moeller et al., 2009; Adams and Wente, 2020), the nuclear retention of mRNAs via Mex67-AA resulted in strongly reduced binding of Dbp5 to the FBA1 mRNA (from a median of approximately eightfold enrichment above background before addition of rapamycin to no enrichment after, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Dbp5 binds to tRNAs independent of known tRNA export proteins and does so in a manner that is distinct from mRNA.
source: Together, these RNA IP experiments suggest that Dbp5 binds to tRNAs independent of known tRNA export proteins and does so in a manner that is distinct from mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from RNA IP experiments showing Dbp5-tRNA interaction independent of Los1, Msn5, and Mex67

claim: The dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G mutants exhibit deficient RNA binding (<5% of WT) and ATPase activity (~10 and 60% of WT, respectively) and have dominant-negative effects on mRNA export status when overexpressed.
source: The dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G mutants have previously been shown to exhibit deficient RNA binding (<5% of WT), ATPase activity (~10 and 60% of WT, respectively) and have a dominant-negative effects on mRNA export status when overexpressed (Hodge et al., 2011, Noble et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: dbp5R369G has elevated Gle1 affinity and effectively competes with WT Dbp5 for Gle1 binding.
source: Additionally, it has been shown that dbp5R369G has elevated Gle1 affinity and effectively competes with WT Dbp5 for Gle1 binding (Hodge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: dbp5E240Q is an ATP hydrolysis mutant that is competent to bind RNA as it is biased to the ATP bound state, but is recessive lethal showing no mRNA export defect when overexpressed in the context of endogenously expressed WT Dbp5.
source: In contrast, dbp5E240Q is an ATP hydrolysis mutant that is competent to bind RNA as it is biased to the ATP bound state, but is recessive lethal showing no mRNA export defect when overexpressed in the context of endogenously expressed WT Dbp5 (Hodge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G mutants localize to the nuclear periphery similar to wild-type Dbp5.
source: The dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G mutants localize to the nuclear periphery similar to wild-type Dbp5; however, dbp5E240Q is predominantly cytoplasmic (with some nuclear envelope localization detectable when wild-type Dbp5 is depleted) (Hodge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: dbp5E240Q is predominantly cytoplasmic (with some nuclear envelope localization detectable when wild-type Dbp5 is depleted).
source: The dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G mutants localize to the nuclear periphery similar to wild-type Dbp5; however, dbp5E240Q is predominantly cytoplasmic (with some nuclear envelope localization detectable when wild-type Dbp5 is depleted) (Hodge et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The ability of Dbp5 to complete ATP hydrolysis (but not RNA binding) is dispensable for pre-ribosomal subunit export, as is Gle1.
source: Unlike the impact of these mutants on mRNA export, it has been reported that the ability of Dbp5 to complete ATP hydrolysis (but not RNA binding) is dispensable for pre-ribosomal subunit export, as is Gle1 (Neumann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Northern blotting targeting tRNAIleUAU revealed both dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G, but not dbp5E240Q, showed an accumulation of intron-containing precursor tRNAIleUAU compared to overexpression of wild-type Dbp5.
source: Northern blotting targeting tRNAIleUAU revealed both dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G, but not dbp5E240Q, showed an accumulation of intron-containing precursor tRNAIleUAU compared to overexpression of wild-type Dbp5 (I/P ratio of 1.97 ± 0.06 vs 1.93 ± 0.31 vs 1.32 ± 0.41, respectively) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: Both the ATPase cycle and regulation of Dbp5 by Gle1 are central to the function of Dbp5 in tRNA export.
source: Furthermore, these data indicate that both the ATPase cycle and regulation of Dbp5 by Gle1 are central to the function of Dbp5 in tRNA export, as each activity is in mRNA export.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing dominant-negative effects of dbp5R426Q and dbp5R369G on tRNA export

claim: Dbp5 binding to ssRNA is linked to the nucleotide state of the enzyme, with the highest affinity for ssRNA occurring when Dbp5 is ATP bound.
source: Previous studies have characterized Dbp5 binding to single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) substrates and demonstrated Dbp5 binding to ssRNA is linked to the nucleotide state of the enzyme, with the highest affinity for ssRNA occurring when Dbp5 is ATP bound (Weirich et al., 2006; Montpetit et al., 2011; Arul Nambi Rajan and Montpetit, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP results in a reduction in the affinity of Dbp5 for the ssRNA substrate.
source: Following ssRNA binding, hydrolysis of ATP to ADP results in a reduction in the affinity of Dbp5 for the ssRNA substrate (Weirich et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Dbp5 generated band shifts for both mixed tRNA substrates and Phe tRNA in the presence of the ATP state analog ADP•BeF3.
source: Consistent with published observations of complex formation between Dbp5 and ssRNA (Weirich et al., 2006; Montpetit et al., 2011), Dbp5 generated band shifts for both mixed tRNA substrates and Phe tRNA in the presence of the ATP state analog ADP•BeF3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In the presence of ATP or ADP, or with no nucleotide, Dbp5 failed to form a band shift with tRNA.
source: In the presence of ATP or ADP, or with no nucleotide, Dbp5 failed to form a similar band shift, which exactly parallels reported interactions between Dbp5 and ssRNA in these nucleotide states (Weirich et al., 2006; Montpetit et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from EMSA experiments

claim: An estimated Kd of ~150 nM (Phe tRNA) and ~130 nM (mixed tRNA) was obtained for Dbp5 binding to tRNA.
source: From quantification of EMSAs, an estimated Kd of ~150 nM (Phe tRNA) and ~130 nM (mixed tRNA) was obtained (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Increasing concentrations of unlabeled tRNA or an ssRNA homopolymeric polyadenylic acid (pA) were found to compete with a fluorescently labeled ssRNA for Dbp5 in the presence of ADP•BeF3.
source: In these assays, increasing concentrations of unlabeled tRNA or an ssRNA homopolymeric polyadenylic acid (pA, routinely used for RNA activation in steady-state ATPase assays; Weirich et al., 2006) were found to compete with a fluorescently labeled ssRNA for Dbp5 in the presence of ADP•BeF3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Dbp5 interacts directly with tRNA in vitro and does so in a manner governed by principles that resemble Dbp5-ssRNA binding.
source: These data, from orthogonal approaches, indicate that Dbp5 interacts directly with tRNA in vitro and does so in a manner governed by principles that resemble Dbp5-ssRNA binding.
evidence: Inferred from EMSA and fluorescence polarization data

claim: Unlike an ssRNA substrate (i.e., pA) that can maximally stimulate ATP turnover to ~0.5 ATP/s, neither tRNA nor poly(I:C) stimulated Dbp5 ATPase activity over a range of RNA concentrations.
source: Unlike an ssRNA substrate (i.e., pA) that can maximally stimulate ATP turnover to ~0.5 ATP/s, neither tRNA nor poly(I:C) (used as an orthogonal dsRNA substrate) stimulated Dbp5 ATPase activity over a range of RNA concentrations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Dbp5 can engage structured and dsRNA substrates, but this does not lead to productive ATP hydrolysis.
source: These results with the above binding data suggest Dbp5 can engage structured and dsRNA substrates, but this does not lead to productive ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: Inferred from binding data and ATPase assay data

claim: Addition of Gle1/InsP6 maximally stimulated Dbp5 (1.03 ± 0.04 ATP/s) to a level like that of ssRNA (1.11 ± 0.07) in the context of tRNA.
source: In the context of tRNA, addition of Gle1/InsP6 maximally stimulated Dbp5 (1.03 ± 0.04 ATP/s) to a level like that of ssRNA (1.11 ± 0.07) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The synergistic activation of Dbp5 ATPase activity by Gle1/InsP6 and tRNA is mirrored by poly(I:C) and observed with both mixed yeast tRNAs as well as yeast phenylalanine tRNA.
source: The synergistic activation of Dbp5 ATPase activity by Gle1/InsP6 and tRNA is mirrored by poly(I:C) and observed with both mixed yeast tRNAs as well as yeast phenylalanine tRNA (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: RNase T1 treatment of the ssRNA (pA) resulted in the loss of RNA-stimulated Dbp5 ATPase activity.
source: As expected, treatment of the ssRNA (pA) with RNase T1 resulted in the loss of RNA-stimulated Dbp5 ATPase activity (0.68 ± 0.06 before RNase T1 treatment to 0.17 ± 0.01 after).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNase T1 treatment experiments

claim: RNase T1 treatment reduced pA/Gle1/InsP6 activation to that of Dbp5 and Gle1/InsP6 alone.
source: Furthermore, RNase T1 treatment reduced pA/Gle1/InsP6 activation (0.98 ± 0.17 before treatment to 0.69 ± 0.07 after) to that of Dbp5 and Gle1/InsP6 alone (0.62 ± 0.03) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: RNase T1-treated tRNA remained unchanged in the ability to activate Dbp5 in the presence of Gle1/InsP6.
source: However, RNase T1-treated tRNA remained unchanged in the ability to activate Dbp5 in the presence of Gle1/InsP6 (1.19 + 0.11 without vs 1.18 ± 0.19 ATP/s with RNase T1 treatment).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNase T1 treatment experiments

claim: RNase T1-treated poly(I:C) remained unchanged in the ability to activate Dbp5 in the presence of Gle1/InsP6.
source: This was recapitulated with poly(I:C) (1.26 ± 0.11 ATP/s without and 1.46 ± 0.135 ATP/s with RNase T1), confirming that the synergistic activation of Dbp5 observed in the presence of Gle1/InsP6 is dependent on the structured tRNA or dsRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNase T1 treatment experiments

claim: The synergistic activation of Dbp5 observed in the presence of Gle1/InsP6 is dependent on the structured tRNA or dsRNA.
source: This was recapitulated with poly(I:C) (1.26 ± 0.11 ATP/s without and 1.46 ± 0.135 ATP/s with RNase T1), confirming that the synergistic activation of Dbp5 observed in the presence of Gle1/InsP6 is dependent on the structured tRNA or dsRNA.
evidence: Inferred from RNase T1 treatment experiments showing no change in activation with structured RNA

claim: Dbp5 may engage tRNA in the cell without ATPase activation and could remain bound until the Dbp5-tRNA complex reaches Gle1 at the cytoplasmic side of an NPC.
source: These findings provide for the possibility that Dbp5 engages tRNA in the cell without ATPase activation and could remain bound until the Dbp5-tRNA complex reaches Gle1 at the cytoplasmic side of an NPC.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of biochemical data

claim: A strong additive defect in pre-tRNAIleUAU processing was observed by northern blotting when los1Δ was combined gle1-4 (approximately fivefold increase in the I/P ratio relative to los1Δ alone) after a 4 hr incubation at 37°C.
source: In support of this model, a strong additive defect in pre- tRNAIleUAU processing was observed by northern blotting when los1Δ was combined gle1-4 (approximately fivefold increase in the I/P ratio relative to los1Δ alone, Figure 5D and E) after a 4 hr incubation at 37°C.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: Gle1, like Dbp5, supports pre-tRNA export independent of Los1.
source: These data indicate that Gle1, like Dbp5, supports pre-tRNA export independent of Los1.
evidence: Inferred from additive defects in los1Δ gle1-4 double mutants

claim: Dbp5 and Gle1 have functions independent of Los1 in tRNA export.
source: Here, a combination of in vivo and in vitro data provides evidence that (1) Dbp5 and Gle1 have functions independent of Los1 in tRNA export
evidence: Supported by genetic and biochemical data presented in the study

claim: Dbp5 can bind tRNA directly in vitro and does so in a manner that does not require Los1, Msn5, and Mex67 in vivo.
source: Here, a combination of in vivo and in vitro data provides evidence that (1) Dbp5 and Gle1 have functions independent of Los1 in tRNA export; (2) Dbp5 can bind tRNA directly in vitro and does so in a manner that does not require Los1, Msn5, and Mex67 in vivo
evidence: Supported by RNA IP and EMSA data presented in the study

claim: The Dbp5 ATPase cycle is uniquely modulated by Gle1/InsP6 in the presence of structured RNA (e.g., tRNA or dsRNA) in vitro and the ATPase cycle supports tRNA export in vivo.
source: Here, a combination of in vivo and in vitro data provides evidence that (1) Dbp5 and Gle1 have functions independent of Los1 in tRNA export; (2) Dbp5 can bind tRNA directly in vitro and does so in a manner that does not require Los1, Msn5, and Mex67 in vivo; and (3) the Dbp5 ATPase cycle is uniquely modulated by Gle1/InsP6 in the presence of structured RNA (e.g., tRNA or dsRNA) in vitro and the ATPase cycle supports tRNA export in vivo.
evidence: Supported by ATPase assay data and dominant-negative mutant data presented in the study

claim: DEAD-box proteins (including Dbp5) broadly interact with RNA via the phosphate backbone.
source: DEAD-box proteins (including Dbp5) broadly interact with RNA via the phosphate backbone (Andersen et al., 2006; Andersen et al., 2006; Linder, 2006; Sengoku et al., 2006; Linder and Fuller-Pace, 2013, Arul Nambi Rajan and Montpetit, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 may bind and travel with a tRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm.
source: First, it may be that Dbp5 binds tRNA to form an inhibited intermediate that is relieved by Gle1/InsP6. This is an attractive hypothesis that is unique from how Dbp5 engages ssRNA (e.g., mRNA) and potentially supports previously proposed export models that suggest Dbp5 may bind and travel with a tRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm (Lari et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of biochemical data and reference to previous model

claim: Gle1/InsP6 may enhance the affinity of Dbp5 for tRNA and 'non-mRNA' substrates.
source: A second possibility is that Gle1/InsP6 enhances the affinity of Dbp5 for tRNA and 'non-mRNA' substrates, which is supported by biochemical characterizations that show Gle1/InsP6 promotes a shift in the steady-state distribution of populated Dbp5 intermediates from weak to strong RNA-binding states (Hodge et al., 2011, Montpetit et al., 2011; Noble et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2018; Gray et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 was previously reported to not bind dsRNA substrates.
source: Moreover, Dbp5 was previously reported to not bind dsRNA substrates (Weirich et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: It has been reported previously that tRNA fails to stimulate Dbp5 ATPase cycle.
source: While it has been reported previously that tRNA fails to stimulate Dbp5 ATPase cycle (Tseng et al., 1998), here it is shown that despite a lack of stimulation when Gle1/InsP6 is absent, Dbp5 is able to bind tRNA in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In mRNA export it is thought that Dbp5 functions are localized at NPCs.
source: For example, in mRNA export it is thought that Dbp5 functions are localized at NPCs (Derrer et al., 2019; Lari et al., 2019; Adams and Wente, 2020), where the Dbp5 ATPase cycle is tightly regulated by co-factors Nup159 and Gle1/InsP6 (Hodge et al., 1999; Rollenhagen et al., 2004; Hodge et al., 2011, Montpetit et al., 2011; Noble et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The essential function of both Dbp5 and Mex67 in mRNA export can be accomplished when these proteins are fused to nuclear pore components.
source: In fact, recent studies have shown the essential function of both Dbp5 and Mex67 in mRNA export can be accomplished when these proteins are fused to nuclear pore components; in addition, Dbp5 does not form a complex with mRNAs in the nucleus (Derrer et al., 2019; Adams and Wente, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 does not form a complex with mRNAs in the nucleus.
source: In fact, recent studies have shown the essential function of both Dbp5 and Mex67 in mRNA export can be accomplished when these proteins are fused to nuclear pore components; in addition, Dbp5 does not form a complex with mRNAs in the nucleus (Derrer et al., 2019; Adams and Wente, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 likely engages mRNAs after they exit the NPC transport channel to direct the final step(s) of mRNA export.
source: These reports suggest that Dbp5 does not travel with an mRNA from the nucleoplasm to the cytoplasmic face of an NPC as part of an mRNA-protein complex; rather, Dbp5 likely engages mRNAs after they exit the NPC transport channel to direct the final step(s) of mRNA export (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from published reports and illustrated in Figure 6

claim: Dbp5 may enter the nucleus to stably engage tRNA and direct events leading to export, following which Dbp5 is removed from the tRNA by Gle1/InsP6 upon nuclear exit.
source: However, in contrast to this mRNA export model, the unique ability of Dbp5 to bind tRNA without ATP stimulation, and then be fully activated by Gle1/InsP6, presents the potential for a novel mechanism of function in regulating tRNA export. Namely, that Dbp5 may enter the nucleus to stably engage tRNA and direct events leading to export, following which Dbp5 is removed from the tRNA by Gle1/InsP6 upon nuclear exit (Figure 6).
evidence: Speculative model based on biochemical data and illustrated in Figure 6

claim: In both mRNA and tRNA export, Gle1/InsP6 activation is required to stimulate ATPase activity and recycle the enzyme.
source: Importantly, in both mRNA and tRNA export, Gle1/InsP6 activation is required to stimulate ATPase activity and recycle the enzyme.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and established knowledge of mRNA export

claim: Dbp5 ATPase activity and Gle1 have been shown to be dispensable for pre-ribosomal subunit transport.
source: In contrast, Dbp5 ATPase activity and Gle1 have been shown to be dispensable for pre-ribosomal subunit transport (Neumann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Lack of RNA-mediated ATPase stimulation following RNA binding may lead to the formation of tRNA-bound intermediates that act as adapters for recruitment of yet to be identified transport factors.
source: Data from this study support a model in which Dbp5-mediated export of both mRNA and tRNA require Gle1/InsP6 activation to remodel RNPs at the cytoplasmic face of the nuclear pore complex (NPC). For tRNA export, lack of RNA-mediated ATPase stimulation following RNA binding may lead to the formation of tRNA-bound intermediates that act as adapters for recruitment of yet to be identified transport factors.

claim: It has been proposed that Dbp5 displaces mRNA export factors such as Mex67 and Nab2 to promote directionality of mRNA transit.
source: In mRNA export, it has been proposed that Dbp5 displaces mRNA export factors such as Mex67 and Nab2 to promote directionality of mRNA transit (Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Tran et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Dbp5 and Mex67 have been proposed to form physical interactions, with Mex67 serving as an adaptor to direct Dbp5 to appropriate mRNA sites for remodeling.
source: Dbp5 and Mex67 have been proposed to form physical interactions, with Mex67 serving as an adaptor to direct Dbp5 to appropriate mRNA sites for remodeling (Lund and Guthrie, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mex67 likely requires an unknown adaptor to form its reported interactions with its tRNA substrates.
source: While Dbp5 recruitment to tRNA does not require Mex67, the data presented in this study do not exclude the possibility that the two proteins co-function to promote tRNA export. Indeed, previously published data suggests Mex67 likely requires an unknown adaptor to form its reported interactions with its tRNA substrates (Yao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Nuclear Dbp5 may promote recruitment of Mex67 or Crm1 to tRNA-protein complexes.
source: Given the in vitro properties of Dbp5 binding to tRNA, it is tempting to speculate that nuclear Dbp5 promotes recruitment of Mex67 or Crm1 to tRNA-protein complexes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental data

claim: The exon junction complex (EJC) and the DEAD-box protein at its core, eIF4AIII, acts as a platform for the binding of other proteins to an mRNA.
source: Indeed, a similar phenomenon has been described for the exon junction complex (EJC) and the DEAD-box protein at its core, eIF4AIII, that acts as a platform for the binding of other proteins to an mRNA (Ballut et al., 2005; Andersen et al., 2006; Bono et al., 2006; Pacheco-Fiallos et al., 2023).

claim: Stable binding of the EJC is governed by trans-acting proteins that lock the complex on the mRNA by stabilizing an ADP-Pi hydrolysis immediate.

claim: Several DEAD-box proteins such as Dbp2 have been reported to bind diverse nucleic acid substrates (ncRNA and mRNA), including G-Quadraplexes, and have roles in R-loop biology.
source: Furthermore, several DEAD-box proteins such as Dbp2 have been reported to bind diverse nucleic acid substrates (ncRNA and mRNA), including G-Quadraplexes, and have roles in R-loop biology (Ma et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2017; Tedeschi et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Lai et al., 2019; Lai and Tran, 2021; Yan et al., 2021; Song et al., 2022).

claim: Other DEAD-box proteins may also demonstrate substrate-specific regulation.
source: Given the high degree of conservation in the structure, function, and regulation of Dbp5 with other DEAD-box proteins (Ozgur et al., 2015; Sloan and Bohnsack, 2018), the observations reported here raise the possibility that other DEAD-box proteins may also demonstrate substrate-specific regulation.

claim: Gle1 and the small molecule InsP6 are potent regulators of Dbp5 activity in multiple RNA export pathways.
source: Furthermore, the results here support the importance of Gle1 and the small molecule InsP6 as potent regulators of Dbp5 activity in multiple RNA export pathways.

claim: Both Dbp5 and Mex67 have general functions in RNA export.
source: Overall, this study and other recent publications support a general function for both Dbp5 and Mex67 in RNA export (Yao et al., 2007; Yao et al., 2008; Faza et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014; Neumann et al., 2016; Chatterjee et al., 2017; Becker et al., 2019; Lari et al., 2019; Nostramo and Hopper, 2020; Vasianovich et al., 2020; Chatterjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study and multiple citations to published literature

claim: It is important to reconsider Dbp5 and Mex67 as general RNA export factors.
source: While these factors have been most well characterized in mRNA export, it is now important to reconsider Dbp5 and Mex67 as general RNA export factors, which raises questions about the possible co-regulation of mRNA and non-coding RNA export pathways to fine-tune gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and published literature
